Principal Components Analysis (PCA) Image Compressor

Image Compression Function

# Initialize compression function
pca_compress <- function(img_matrix, k){
  img_pca <- prcomp(img_matrix, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE) # Perform PCA on img_matrix
  scores <- img_pca$x[, 1:k] # Extract first k PC scores
  eigenvectors <- img_pca$rotation[, 1:k] # Extract first k eigenvectors
  comp_img <- scores %*% t(eigenvectors) # Obtain rank k approximation of img_matrix
  error <- norm((img_matrix - comp_img), type = "F") # Calculate error of rank k approx.
  return(list(img = comp_img, error = error))
}

Image 1

Original Image vs. Ranks 1-10 Approximation

Approximation Error

First Eigenvector

Interpretation: The weights from the first eigenvector for Image 1 are randomly distributed around zero, meaning that there are trade-offs between the variables’ impacts on the first principal component.

First PC Score

Interpretation: The values from the first PC score for Image 1 are all negative and appear mostly randomly distributed between certain intervals (such as between -18 and -20, or between -20.5 and -22). There is a distinct gap around -17.5, dividing the scores into subgroups, which implies that the image’s data may also be divided into subgroups that share similar characteristics.

Conclusion

I would argue that the rank k at which the approximation of Image 1 is “sufficiently good” is around k = 60, as it appears to capture the general graininess of the original image.

Image 2

Original Image vs. Ranks 1-10 Approximation

Approximation Error

First Eigenvector

Interpretation: The bar plot of the weights from the first eigenvector for Image 2 decrease in a constant manner, implying that the variables are ordered from least to most impactful in determining the first principal component.

First PC Score

Interpretation: The graph of the first PC score values for Image 2 are evenly and randomly distributed around 0, meaning that PC1 is largely capturing the data’s trend.

Conclusion

I would argue that the rank k at which the approximation of Image 2 is “sufficiently good” is at k = 2. The rank 1 approximation has some error, but for k > 1, there is virtually 0 error, and the image essentially perfectly matches the original.

Image 3

Original Image vs. Ranks 1-10 Approximation

Approximation Error

First Eigenvector

Interpretation: All of the weights from Image 3’s first eigenvector are negative, meaning that all of the variables contribute inversely to the first principal component.

First PC Score

Interpretation: The graph of the first PC score values for Image 3 follows a distinct curve, which may imply that the image’s data follows a specific trend, rather than subgroups or clusters.

Conclusion

I would argue that the rank k at which the approximation of Image 3 is “sufficiently good” is at k = 50. The image is fairly clear, and the approximation error occurs just after the elbow of the error graph.

Image 4

Original Image vs. Ranks 1-10 Approximation

Approximation Error

First Eigenvector

Interpretation: The weights from the first eigenvector for Image 4 are primarily negative, though the bars curve above zero for a small portion of the graph. This implies that some of the image’s variables have inverse relationships with each other, though a large amount of the variables contribute inversely to the principal component score.

First PC Score

Interpretation: The graph of the first PC score values for Image 3 follows a distinct curve, which may imply that the image’s data follows a specific trend, rather than subgroups or clusters.

Conclusion

I would argue that the rank k at which the approximation of Image 4 is “sufficiently good” is at k = 20.
